t: Splitting a String Into Descending Consecutive Values — Editorial
o: We must cut the digit string into at least two contiguous pieces so that, read as numbers (leading zeros ignored, e.g. "0090" is 90), each piece is exactly one less than the piece before it. For "1234" no split works: the natural cut [1, 2, 3, 4] ascends, and regroupings such as [12, 34] do not descend by exactly 1 either. For "050043" the split ["05", "004", "3"] reads [5, 4, 3], which is valid. The structural key is that once the first piece is chosen, the VALUE of every later piece is forced (previous minus one); only how many leading zeros pad it can vary. Since the string has at most 20 characters, enumerating candidate first pieces and backtracking — or a polynomial DP over cut points — is easily affordable.
k: Leading zeros change only the width, not the value: "05" and "005" both represent 5.
After picking the first number the chain is forced — each next piece must equal the previous value minus 1.
With n <= 20, exhaustive backtracking is fast; a value-set DP over cut boundaries gives a tidy polynomial bound.

a.n: Approach 1: Exhaustive Backtracking Over Cut Points
a.i: Try every possible end index of the first piece; from each seed value, recursively try every way to cut the remaining suffix so the next piece is exactly one less than the current value. Reaching the end of the string certifies that every piece (at least two of them) satisfied the descending-by-one rule.
s: For each j from 1 to n-1, seed with the first piece value v = int(s[0..j)).
Recurse: at position i expecting target t, try every j > i with int(s[i..j)) == t and continue from j with target t-1.
Succeed when a call consumes the whole string (i == n).
Return true if any seed succeeds, else false.
a.t: Exponential in the worst case (each cut point branches), but with n <= 20 it runs in microseconds
a.sp: O(n) — recursion depth plus substring temporaries

a.n: Approach 2: Dynamic Programming Over Cut Boundaries
a.i: Let dp[j] be the set of values v such that some valid descending chain covers the prefix ending at cut j. Seed dp[j] with the value of the whole prefix s[0..j) — that prefix is the forced first piece — then relax: a piece s[i..j) with value w extends a chain ending at i exactly when w equals some v - 1 with v in dp[i]. The answer is dp[n] being non-empty, which by construction requires at least two pieces.
s: Create dp[0..n] as empty hash sets.
Seed dp[j] = { int(s[0..j)) } for 1 <= j <= n-1.
For every boundary i and end j > i, let w = int(s[i..j)); if w + 1 is in dp[i], insert w into dp[j].
Return true iff dp[n] is non-empty.
a.t: O(n^3) — O(n^2) boundary pairs, each with an O(n)-length numeric parse; trivial for n <= 20
a.sp: O(n^2) — up to O(n^2) distinct values stored across all boundary sets

w: Lead with the backtracking sketch, then offer the DP if asked for a guaranteed polynomial bound. Pitfalls: forgetting the split needs TWO or more pieces (never seed the full-length prefix), relaxing "descending by exactly 1" into "merely non-increasing", and misreading all-zero inputs like "001" where repeated values are not consecutive-descending. Follow-ups: reconstruct an actual valid split (store parent pointers in the DP) or scale to length 10^5, where the forced-chain structure means you mostly need the first piece plus zero-padding checks.
